narrative:
The system estimates there’s a 50% chance you’ll leave your job in the near future—well above the 40% threshold that triggers caution. Because of this elevated risk, the promotion was denied. The decision wasn’t based on personal traits like gender, age, or health, but on patterns seen across similar employees in the private sector.

Three factors stood out. First, you haven’t received other job offers while working here. Employees who stay often have outside opportunities, suggesting they’re actively sought after; the lack of offers in your case slightly increased the risk of leaving. Second, you’ve spent 6–10 years in your current role. While this shows loyalty, it also means you’ve reached a point where many employees start looking for new challenges, pushing the risk higher. Finally, your 6–10 years of total work experience also nudged the prediction upward, as employees with this level of experience often seek growth that may not be available in their current position.

Other signals reinforce this picture. You feel you haven’t received the promotion you deserve, aren’t emotionally committed to the organization, and struggle with work-life balance—all common signs of disengagement. On the positive side, you’ve benefited from training and are satisfied with your work environment, which slightly reduces the risk.

To improve your chances next time, focus on deepening your connection to the organization. Seek projects that align with your long-term goals, discuss career development with your manager, and explore ways to restore work-life balance. Addressing these areas can lower the perceived risk of leaving and strengthen your case for future opportunities.
